Altruistic provers generate execution proofs and propagate them over p2p so that consensus layer (CL) nodes can validate execution payloads statelessly without re-executing them. It is a fully opt-in design that does not change consensus validity rules, and is regarded as the first step of the zkEVM roadmap. At ACDC #189 (2026-10-15) it failed to be promoted to CFI because of insufficient CL team support and was marked DFI (declined) for Hegotá. 28httsigkqz: EIP-8363 Tapered Issuance Burn is a proposal to deduct and burn a set share of the ideal reward each epoch for each duty a validator is assigned, namely attestation, block proposal, and sync committee participation. The burn rate grows linearly with the staking ratio and reaches 100% at a fixed saturation balance, so the net staking yield falls as staking grows. The proposers argue that in the current curve the yield falls only in inverse proportion to the square root of the staking ratio and has a floor of about 1.5%, so there is no point at which the staking incentive switches off. They explain that introducing the burn lets the staking market find equilibrium where the yield meets the risk premium that stakers require, that this point lies below a 50% staking ratio, and that above it issuance no longer induces stake growth. Applying it in full at the fork would cause the yield to plunge at the current staking ratio, so BASE_REWARD_FACTOR is temporarily raised and the burn is phased in over 18 months, while the shape of the curve, which does not reward growth beyond 50%, takes effect from the first day of activation. By the figures quoted on Twitter, the net consensus yield falls from 2.6% to 1.2% at current staking levels, and the first-day reduction is 13%. The authors are pintail, Jérôme de Tychey, dapplion, pa7x1, Ladislaus von Daniels, and Justin Drake. The core principle rests on pa7x1's prior research, and the refinement of per-duty burning rests on research by Anders Elowsson. According to the EIP document the date of writing is July 14, 2026, and it was submitted to ethereum/EIPs on August 4, 2026, which opened the Magicians thread, and its status is Draft. The proposer's tweet on the day of submission listed it as EIP-8361, and it was later cleaned up to 8363. The submission came 48 hours before the PFI deadline for the Hegotá fork, and in the thread gregk pointed out that there was not enough time to review a monetary policy change of this size, and that on the strawmap, issuance changes were expected to be handled in an I* fork. De Tychey replied that PFI is not scheduled inclusion but the start of feedback, and that if the validator entry queue stays full at its limit, more than 70 million ETH will be staked by January 1, 2028, so waiting for I* is effectively the same as giving up on the change. Because it is a consensus layer change, a hard fork is required. On September 2, a separate research proposal thread on how validator control changes if EIP-8363 works was also posted on Magicians.

2dli0btqj6n: EIP-8130 is an account abstraction approach proposed in October 2025 by Chris Hunter of Coinbase. It introduces a new transaction type 0x79 and a keystore system contract at a deterministic address, and registers which key holds which permissions for each account. The core of the design is to make secp256k1, P-256, passkeys (WebAuthn), and delegation native authenticators built into the protocol, so that nodes can tell which verification is required without executing wallet code. In the L1 profile, the set of native authenticators can only be extended through a hard fork. On the other side, EIP-8141 (frame transactions) splits a single transaction into up to 64 frames and handles verification, gas payment, sender identification, and replay protection in EVM code, so that it can absorb new signature schemes without a new transaction type. Tempo is a payments chain in the Stripe family, and its transaction design sits on the side that reduces the knobs to tune even further. The debate began on August 25, 2026, when Derek Chiang posted a piece comparing frames and 8130. Currently L1 has listed 8141 as a scheduled item for the Hegotá upgrade, while Base plans to ship 8130 in its September Cobalt upgrade and is testing it on the Vibenet devnet.

Its purpose is to let contracts be deployed deterministically to the same address across multiple chains. The authors are Francisco Giordano, Toni Wahrstätter, Nick Johnson, and Jochem Brouwer, and its status is Last Call. This factory has so far been deployed via a keyless transaction created using Nick's method. But that transaction has a fixed gas price and limit, so it often couldn't be deployed on chains whose gas parameters didn't match. According to the EIP body, as gas schedules have changed, this same problem has started appearing on Ethereum and its devnets too. So this EIP ensures the factory is present on the chain, whether deployed via a regular transaction or included in genesis.

faipe2tj40: EIP-8037 (Increase Gas Costs for State Growth) proposes raising the gas cost of state-growing operations so that state doesn't grow excessively even as block gas limits rise. It introduces a cost per state byte (CPSB) and meters state-growth costs separately. EIP-8038 (Update Gas Costs for State Access) raises the gas cost of state-access operations. Both EIPs are in Last Call. According to nero_eth, core developers delayed the Glamsterdam fork on the Hoodi testnet while reviewing the ChainSecurity report. It was already known that contracts hardcoding forwarded gas would be affected by repricing. What's newly revealed is that gas already spent can be refunded mid-transaction, increasing gasleft(). That can cause the gas counter measured before and after a call to underflow and revert, or let a failed subcall refund gas in a way that executes a path that should have been unreachable, making the transaction appear to succeed. Because the state gas reservoir isn't visible during execution, gas usage measured by the GAS difference before and after a call could also come out lower than actual usage. nero_eth said coordination among the parties involved could resolve this, but in the worst case the spec itself may need to change.

nayjiixuia:
Summary of the recent Binance hack and EIP-7702 wallets

1. 7702 itself is not broken. You don't need to be afraid of using wallets that support 7702, such as MetaMask or Uniswap.

2. 7702 is a feature that adds smart functions to an ordinary wallet so that approval and transfer are handled at once. That is what makes swaps possible with a single click.

3. The problem is that hackers can also use this feature to drain a wallet all at once. In this Binance case, the hacker pulled out 64 tokens including ETH and USDT in one transaction. Without 7702, each coin would have had to be sent separately.

4. On top of that, Binance was continuing to make withdrawals from the compromised wallet, so if the hacker had sent them separately, the transaction ordering would have tangled and many would have failed. 7702 let them take as much as possible, as fast as possible.

5. But to use 7702, the hacker either already had the private key or tricked Binance into giving a 7702 signature. The latter would require Binance to be extremely sloppy, so it is unlikely, but given how things are going these days, it is hard to say the chance is zero.

6. Wallet developers must never create a channel through which 7702 signatures can be requested from outside. Companies that run hot wallets, such as exchanges, must not create such a channel even for internal use. Ordinary users only need to use well-known wallets.

7. 7702 is a transitional feature, and once the final goal, EIP-8141 (Frame Transactions), arrives, wallets can be set up far more safely. For example, a safeguard such as 'transfers above 1000 ETH require an additional signature' can be set on the wallet itself.

8. Ultimately, getting both security and convenience is the end goal of Ethereum UX, but there is still a long way to go. For now it is closer to a problem of the transitional state.

Conclusion: the problem is that the all-in-one wallet's private key was stolen, not the wallet.

p1nvq2gw51: EIP-7702 (Set Code for EOAs), proposed by Vitalik Buterin, Sam Wilson, Ansgar Dietrichs, and lightclient and now in Final status, lets an externally owned account (EOA) delegate smart contract code to its own account through a special signature called a '7702 authorization', enabling batching that bundles approve and transfer into one transaction. In the Binance hack, the hacker used this feature to drain 64 tokens including ETH and USDT in a single transaction. Without 7702, each token would have needed a separate transaction, and many would likely have failed while competing for the nonce with legitimate withdrawal transactions. EIP-8141 (Frame Transaction, Draft), which decentrek named as the endgame, is an account abstraction proposal that builds accounts only from multisig contracts and lets post-conditions such as 'no transfer above 1000 ETH without an additional signature' be set on the transfer function. EIP-8141 is currently being tested on bogota-devnet-1.

wamujmqnqy: EIP-8141 (Frame Transaction) is a draft written by Vitalik Buterin, lightclient, Derek Chiang, and others. It splits a transaction into a sequence of frames, which are contract calls responsible for verification, gas payment authorization, and execution, letting users define their own verification and gas payment methods. EIP-8130 (Keystore Accounts) is a draft written by Coinbase's Chris Hunter. It registers, for each account, an actor bound to an authenticator contract that verifies signatures, and nodes filter transactions using a standard set of authenticators instead of simulating arbitrary EVM code. 8141 caps the gas for the verification step at MAX_VERIFY_GAS in the public mempool. EIP-8250 (keyed nonce) and EIP-8272 (recent root) are companion proposals that layer privacy use cases on top of 8141. At the late-August ACDE meeting, 8141 was SFI'd (Scheduled For Inclusion) into the Hegotá hard fork.
